hops.afterHeading: The illusion, and the rule it reveals
hops.title: Wrist vibrators that shrank seventeen waists
hops.text: Seventeen volunteers, selected from 24 because they felt the illusion reliably, lay blindfolded in a brain scanner with both palms flat against the sides of their waist. Researchers then buzzed the extensor tendons on the back of both wrists at about 110 Hz. All 17 felt their wrists bending inward, and their waist shrinking with them. In a test before the scans, their reproduced wrist movements corresponded to an average apparent narrowing of 9.4 centimeters, about 28 percent of waist width. Touch said the palms were still on the hips; the spindles said the wrists were flexing. The brain resolved the conflict by recalibrating the felt size of the waist.

sources.citation: Ehrsson HH, Kito T, Sadato N, Passingham RE, Naito E (2005), PLoS Biology 3(12):e412.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A blindfolded student resting both palms on their waist while their shadow on the wall shows a much narrower waist.
image.caption: When wrist spindles report inward bending but the hands stay on the hips, the brain shrinks the felt waist.

hops.title: Too much vitamin B6 and the lost sense of position
hops.text: In 1983, neurologists described seven adults who had become badly unsteady while taking high amounts of supplemental vitamin B6, with maximum daily intakes of 2 to 6 grams; four could no longer walk. Their sense of joint position was severely impaired, and in a later case balance got much worse in the dark. Yet muscle strength stayed normal and the central nervous system was clinically spared: the damage fell mainly on sensory neurons. Like I.W. and the two people with inactivating PIEZO2 variants, they separate losing the sense of position from losing the power to move. All seven improved after stopping the supplement.

sources.citation: Schaumburg H, Kaplan J, Windebank A, Vick N, Rasmus S, Pleasure D, Brown MJ (1983), New England Journal of Medicine 309(8):445-448.
EFSA Panel on Nutrition, Novel Foods and Food Allergens (2023), EFSA Journal 21(5):e08006.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: An amber bottle tipped on its side with small yellow tablets and a glass of water on a kitchen counter.
image.caption: Excess vitamin B6 damaged sensory nerves, so balance suffered in the dark while muscle strength held up.

hops.title: The small box that feels heavier
hops.text: Here is one to try with two cardboard boxes, one small and one much larger. Add things to the small one until a kitchen scale says both weigh the same, close the lids, and lift them in turn. The small box feels heavier, even though you packed it yourself. Randall Flanagan and Michael Beltzner had volunteers lift equally heavy large and small objects in alternation, over and over, until they scaled their fingertip forces precisely to the true weights. The smaller object still felt heavier. The authors concluded that high-level cognitive and perceptual factors can produce the illusion.

sources.citation: Flanagan JR, Beltzner MA (2000), Nature Neuroscience 3(7):737-741.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A puzzled student holding a large cardboard box easily in one hand while a tiny equal-weight box dips lower in the other.
image.caption: Even after your fingers learn how hard to lift two equal-weight boxes, the smaller one still feels heavier.
